## Structural Mapping

| ABCD                                                                          |      XCD | Pattern                                                                   |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------: | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Ch. 1–4: intro, data, distributions, explaining variation                     |  Ch. 1–2 | Condensed into a faster “explore data with R → modeling variation” launch |
| Ch. 5–7 and parts of Ch. 9: empty model, error, group model, regression model |  Ch. 2–3 | Modeling content is pulled earlier and made more streamlined              |
| Ch. 10: Logic of Inference                                                    |    Ch. 4 | Essentially carried forward, renumbered                                   |
| Ch. 11: Model Comparison with F                                               |    Ch. 5 | Essentially carried forward, renumbered                                   |
| Ch. 12: Confidence Intervals                                                  |    Ch. 6 | Essentially carried forward, renumbered                                   |
| Ch. 13–16: Multivariate + Interactions                                        | Ch. 7–10 | Essentially carried forward, renumbered                                   |


## The main transformation

### Compressing Content

:::{.columns}
:::{.column}
#### ABCD
- Part I: Exploring Variation:
  - Ch 1-4 
- Part II: Modeling Variation
  - Ch 5-7 & part of 9
  - Ch 8 is dropped(To be verified)

:::
:::{.column}
#### XCD
- Part I: Exploring and Modeling Variation
  - Ch 1-2 (Exploring)
  - Ch 3-4 (Modeling)
:::

### Example Datasets
:::{.columns}
:::{.column}
#### ABCD
A few datasets (Students, Home-price, ...), but each dominating a chapter or two.
:::
:::{.column}
#### XCD
One coherent dataset (Home-price) used everywhere.

:::

Some Chat GPT observations:

- detailed “understanding data” material from ABCD Chapter 2,
- distributional exploration from ABCD Chapter 3,
- research design / DGP material from ABCD Chapter 4,
- much of ABCD Chapter 6 on variance, standard deviation, z-scores, and the normal model,
- some “digging deeper” group-model material from ABCD Chapter 8.

ABCD includes full chapters on “Examining Distributions,” “Quantifying Error,” and “Digging Deeper into Group Models,” while XCD does not have direct chapter-level equivalents for those.


# Now Approach

Here is the **5-unit XCD lineup** I would use. This keeps the course aligned with XCD’s own structure while preserving your original 29-day course rhythm.

## 5-Unit XCD Approach

| Unit                                            | Approx. Days | XCD Chapters / Sections                                                 | Core Purpose                                                                                                                                 | Assessment                             |
| ----------------------------------------------- | -----------: | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| **Unit 1. Exploring Data and Variation**        |     Days 1–7 | **Ch. 1: 1.1–1.11** and **Ch. 2: 2.1–2.3**                              | R basics, data frames, variable types, data cleaning, one-variable and two-variable visualization                                            | **Exam 1 prep begins**                 |
| **Unit 2. Modeling Variation**                  |    Days 9–16 | **Ch. 2: 2.4–2.10** and **Ch. 3: 3.1–3.13**                             | Empty model, mean as model, error, sums of squares, group model, regression model, ANOVA, PRE, F                                             | **Exam 1 or early Exam 2 content**     |
| **Unit 3. Inference Using P-Values**            |   Days 17–22 | **Ch. 4: 4.1–4.11** and **Ch. 5: 5.1–5.15**                             | Sampling distributions, null model, p-values, t distribution, F distribution, Type I/II error, pairwise comparisons, chi-square independence | **Exam 2**                             |
| **Unit 4. Estimation and Confidence Intervals** |   Days 23–26 | **Ch. 6: 6.1–6.15**                                                     | Bootstrap CIs, standard error, t-based CIs, CIs for $\beta_0$, slope, pairwise comparisons, CI width                                         | CI quiz / applied inference assignment |
| **Unit 5. Multivariate and Interaction Models** |   Days 27–29 | **Ch. 7: 7.1–7.9**, selected **Ch. 8: 8.1–8.11**, optional **Ch. 9–10** | Multivariate models, targeted model comparisons, unique effects, optional interactions                                                       | Final project / final review           |

XCD’s full TOC supports this grouping: Chapter 1 covers R/data/visualization; Chapter 2 moves from two-variable relationships into the empty model and sums of squares; Chapter 3 develops group and regression models with ANOVA, PRE, and F; Chapters 4–5 build p-value inference through sampling distributions, t/F distributions, and chi-square independence; Chapter 6 covers CIs; Chapters 7–10 move into multivariate and interaction models. ([app.coursekata.org][1])

---

## Unit 1 — Exploring Data and Variation

**Days 1–7**
**XCD sections:** Ch. 1 **1.1–1.11** plus Ch. 2 **2.1–2.3**

### Main topics

* Welcome to statistics and data science
* R basics: functions, objects, data frames
* Variable types
* Selecting, filtering, recoding, missing data
* Quantitative summaries and visualizations
* Categorical summaries and visualizations
* Relationships between two variables
* Two-variable visualizations

### Suggested class flow

| Day | XCD Sections | Focus                                                        |
| --: | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
|   1 | 1.1–1.4      | Syllabus, intro to R, functions, objects                     |
|   2 | 1.5–1.7      | Data frames, variable types, select/filter                   |
|   3 | 1.8–1.9      | Missing data, recoding, creating variables                   |
|   4 | 1.10         | Quantitative variables: histograms, boxplots, summaries      |
|   5 | 1.11         | Categorical variables: counts, proportions, bar plots        |
|   6 | 2.1–2.2      | Relationships between two variables; choosing displays       |
|   7 | 2.3 + review | More two-variable visualization; description/modeling bridge |

**Why this unit works:** XCD Chapter 1 is basically the compressed replacement for much of ABCD’s early data, R, and visualization content. Chapter 2 begins with relationships between two variables before moving into modeling, so I would put **2.1–2.3** with Unit 1 rather than Unit 2. ([app.coursekata.org][2])

---

## Unit 2 — Modeling Variation

**Days 9–16**
**XCD sections:** Ch. 2 **2.4–2.10** and Ch. 3 **3.1–3.13**

### Main topics

* Explaining variation in an outcome variable
* Mean as a model
* Empty model
* DATA = MODEL + ERROR
* Parameters and estimates
* Total error and sum of squares
* Group model with categorical explanatory variable
* Regression model with quantitative explanatory variable
* ANOVA tables
* PRE and F

### Suggested class flow

| Day | XCD Sections         | Focus                                                            |
| --: | -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
|   9 | 2.4–2.7              | Explaining variation, mean as model, empty model, error notation |
|  10 | 2.8–2.10             | Parameters/estimates, total error, sum of squares                |
|  11 | Supplemental bridge  | One-mean/empty-model sampling intuition, optional                |
|  12 | Supplemental bridge  | Distribution tools: standard error, normal-ish/t/F preview       |
|  13 | 3.1–3.5              | Group model, GLM notation, group-model error                     |
|  14 | 3.6–3.10             | Regression model, slope/intercept, regression error, ANOVA       |
|  15 | 3.11–3.13            | SS Model, PRE, F                                                 |
|  16 | Review / application | Compare empty, group, and regression models                      |

**Important adjustment:** I would keep Days 11–12, but I would not make them full traditional-statistics detours. Instead, use them as **bridges** that support XCD’s modeling spine. For example, Day 11 can connect the empty model to one-mean inference, and Day 12 can prepare students for simulated vs mathematical sampling distributions.

XCD Chapter 3 is the real modeling hub: it includes the `Neighborhood` model, GLM notation, error reduction, the `HomeSizeK` regression model, ANOVA tables, PRE, and F. ([app.coursekata.org][1])

---

## Unit 3 — Inference Using P-Values

**Days 17–22**
**XCD sections:** Ch. 4 **4.1–4.11** and Ch. 5 **5.1–5.15**

### Main topics

* The problem of inference
* Constructing sampling distributions
* Sampling distribution of $b_1$
* What counts as unlikely
* p-values
* Mathematical model of the sampling distribution of $b_1$
* Hypothesis testing for regression
* Sampling distributions of PRE and F
* F distribution
* Relationship between F and t
* Type I and Type II error
* Multiple groups
* Pairwise comparisons
* Simultaneous comparisons
* Chi-square test of independence

### Suggested class flow

| Day | XCD Sections | Focus                                                                           |
| --: | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
|  17 | 4.1–4.3      | Problem of inference; constructing sampling distribution of $b_1$               |
|  18 | 4.4–4.6      | Unlikely samples, p-value, calculating p-value                                  |
|  19 | 4.7–4.9      | t distribution as mathematical model; regression hypothesis test                |
|  20 | 5.1–5.8      | PRE, F, F distribution, F/t relationship, regression model test                 |
|  21 | 5.9–5.13     | Type I/II error, multiple groups, pairwise comparisons, chi-square independence |
|  22 | Exam 2       | Inference using p-values                                                        |

This is the cleanest place for **Exam 2**, because XCD Chapters 4–5 are the p-value inference sequence. Chapter 4 builds inference from sampling distributions and $b_1$; Chapter 5 generalizes that to PRE, F, multiple groups, pairwise comparisons, simultaneous comparisons, and chi-square independence. ([app.coursekata.org][3])

---

## Unit 4 — Estimation and Confidence Intervals

**Days 23–26**
**XCD sections:** Ch. 6 **6.1–6.15**

### Main topics

* From hypothesis testing to confidence intervals
* Thinking with sampling distributions
* Basic CI logic
* Bootstrapping
* Bootstrap sampling distribution
* Shuffle vs resample
* Standard error
* t-based confidence intervals
* Interpreting CIs
* CIs and model comparison
* CI for $\beta_0$
* CI for regression slope
* Pairwise CIs
* What affects CI width

### Suggested class flow

| Day | XCD Sections | Focus                                                           |
| --: | ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
|  23 | 6.1–6.3      | From p-values to estimation; basic CI logic                     |
|  24 | 6.4–6.6      | Bootstrap CI, bootstrap sampling distribution, standard error   |
|  25 | 6.7–6.9      | t-based CI, interpretation, CIs and model comparison            |
|  26 | 6.10–6.15    | CI for $\beta_0$, slope, pairwise comparisons, CI width, review |

This should be its own unit, not just an add-on after p-values. XCD Chapter 6 explicitly reframes inference from “rejecting the empty model” toward estimating plausible parameter values, then uses bootstrap and t-based approaches to construct confidence intervals. ([app.coursekata.org][4])

---

## Unit 5 — Multivariate and Interaction Models

**Days 27–29**
**XCD sections:** Ch. 7 **7.1–7.9**, selected Ch. 8 **8.1–8.11**, optional Ch. 9–10

### Main topics

* Models with two explanatory variables
* Visualizing multivariate relationships
* Specifying and fitting multivariate models
* Interpreting parameter estimates
* Predictions
* Multivariate residuals, SS, PRE, and F
* Targeted model comparisons
* Unique effects of predictors
* Optional interactions

### Suggested class flow

| Day | XCD Sections        | Focus                                                             |
| --: | ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
|  27 | 7.1–7.5             | Intro to multivariate models; fitting and interpreting            |
|  28 | 7.6–7.9 + 8.1–8.4   | Error, SS, PRE, F; targeted model comparisons                     |
|  29 | 8.5–8.11 or 9.1–9.8 | Predictor selection / multiple predictors / optional interactions |

For a 29-day course, I would **not** try to cover all of Chapters 7–10 in detail. I would make Unit 5 either:

**Option A: Multivariate Core**
Use Ch. 7 and selected Ch. 8 only.

**Option B: Multivariate + One Interaction Day**
Use Ch. 7, selected Ch. 8, and one carefully chosen interaction lesson from Ch. 9.

**Option C: Project-Based Finish**
Use Ch. 7–8 concepts in a final modeling project, with interaction models as optional extensions.

XCD Chapters 7–8 introduce multivariate models, targeted comparisons, sums of squares, PRE, F, inference for targeted comparisons, and models with multiple categorical or quantitative predictors; Chapters 9–10 then extend this to interactions. ([app.coursekata.org][1])

---

## My recommended 5-unit calendar skeleton

| Day Range      | Unit                                        | XCD Coverage                        | Major Product                                   |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| **Days 1–7**   | Unit 1: Exploring Data and Variation        | 1.1–1.11, 2.1–2.3                   | Data/visualization fluency                      |
| **Day 8**      | Exam 1                                      | Units 1 + intro modeling            | Description, visualization, R basics            |
| **Days 9–16**  | Unit 2: Modeling Variation                  | 2.4–2.10, 3.1–3.13                  | Empty/group/regression model comparison         |
| **Days 17–21** | Unit 3: Inference Using P-Values            | 4.1–4.11, 5.1–5.15                  | Sampling distributions, p-values, F, chi-square |
| **Day 22**     | Exam 2                                      | Units 2–3                           | Modeling + p-value inference                    |
| **Days 23–26** | Unit 4: Estimation and Confidence Intervals | 6.1–6.15                            | Bootstrap/t CIs and interpretation              |
| **Days 27–29** | Unit 5: Multivariate and Interaction Models | 7.1–7.9, selected 8.x, optional 9.x | Multivariate application or final project       |

The one decision I would make explicit in the syllabus is this: **Goodness-of-fit, difference of two proportions, and classical one-mean tests are supplemental extensions, not central XCD units.** XCD’s central spine is: **explore variation → fit models → compare models → use sampling distributions for inference → estimate parameters → extend to multivariate models.**

# Detailed Plan
Below is a **working day-by-day activity map** for the 5-unit XCD approach. I used a compact format inside each cell:

**T = Topic**
**C = Content**
**B = Beyond textbook / extension**

I kept the XCD spine aligned to the book: Ch. 1 data/R/visualization; Ch. 2 empty model and error; Ch. 3 group/regression models, PRE, F; Ch. 4–5 p-value inference; Ch. 6 confidence intervals; Ch. 7–8 multivariate models, with optional Ch. 9 interaction material. The XCD TOC supports this sequencing. ([app.coursekata.org][1])

## Dataset suggestions

Your idea to collect a **student survey dataset** is excellent. I would use it repeatedly, but carefully. Keep it low-risk and not too personal.

Good student-survey variables:

| Variable type                       | Examples                                                                                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Quantitative outcome candidates     | weekly study hours, commute time, sleep hours, number of work hours, screen time, exercise minutes                                                         |
| Categorical predictors              | full-time/part-time student, works for pay, online/in-person preference, major group, first-generation status only if optional/sensitive handling is clear |
| Quantitative predictors             | work hours, commute time, number of enrolled units, sleep hours                                                                                            |
| Categorical outcomes for chi-square | prefers online/in-person, uses tutoring yes/no, works for pay yes/no                                                                                       |

I would avoid sensitive variables unless they are clearly optional and aggregated.

Other reliable practical datasets:

| Dataset                       | Best use                                                  |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `mtcars`                      | Early R, group means, regression, model comparison        |
| `iris`                        | Data frames, variable types, group means, visualization   |
| `palmerpenguins`              | Group models, visualization, missing data, regression     |
| `tips`                        | Group differences, regression, multivariate models        |
| `diamonds`                    | Large-data visualization, regression, multivariate models |
| `gapminder`                   | Trend, visualization, multivariate thinking               |
| CourseKata home-price dataset | Best alignment with XCD Ch. 3 and Ch. 7 examples          |

My recommendation: use **student survey data for motivation**, but use **clean traditional datasets for first exposure**. Then return to student data once students understand the operation. That way the course feels relevant without making every lesson depend on messy real data.

A good pattern is:

> First learn the operation on a clean dataset → repeat the operation on student survey data → explain what the result means in a human context.

# Exams Discussions
I would **keep Exam 2**. In fact, XCD almost needs it because the middle of the course has a natural breakpoint after **model comparison + p-value inference**.

I would structure the course around **two midterm-style exams plus a final project**, not replace Exam 2 with the project.

## Recommended assessment structure

| Assessment        |                       Timing | Main focus                                                                                       | Why keep it                                                                               |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------: | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Exam 1**        |                        Day 8 | Data, visualization, R basics, variable types, intro relationships                               | Checks whether students can read data and describe variation before modeling gets serious |
| **Exam 2**        |                       Day 22 | Empty/group/regression models, sampling distributions, p-values, PRE, F, chi-square independence | Checks individual understanding of the central XCD inference arc                          |
| **Final project** | Days 23–29, submitted at end | Confidence intervals, multivariate modeling, interpretation, communication                       | Lets students apply ideas collaboratively without replacing individual accountability     |

So the structure becomes:

| Unit                                 |  Days | Assessment               |
| ------------------------------------ | ----: | ------------------------ |
| Unit 1: Exploring Data and Variation |   1–7 | Exam 1 on Day 8          |
| Unit 2: Modeling Variation           |  9–16 | Included on Exam 2       |
| Unit 3: Inference Using P-Values     | 17–21 | Exam 2 on Day 22         |
| Unit 4: Confidence Intervals         | 23–26 | Project milestone / quiz |
| Unit 5: Multivariate Models          | 27–29 | Final project            |

## Why Exam 2 is worth keeping

Exam 2 gives students a needed checkpoint on the hardest conceptual material:

* What is the empty model?
* What does it mean for one model to reduce error compared to another?
* What are PRE and F measuring?
* What is a sampling distribution?
* What is a p-value?
* What does “under the null model” mean?
* How do we interpret model output?
* What is the difference between statistical significance and practical usefulness?

Those are too important to assess only through group work or completion-based JNBs.

## How to support students before Exam 2

I would build a **three-part support system**.

### 1. Exam 2 review quiz, auto-graded

Give a Canvas quiz after Day 21. Let students take it multiple times.

Recommended structure:

| Item type                                      | Number |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -----: |
| Vocabulary/concept questions                   |    5–6 |
| Interpret model output                         |    4–5 |
| Sampling distribution / p-value interpretation |    4–5 |
| PRE/F/model comparison                         |    3–4 |
| One chi-square or categorical inference item   |    1–2 |

Make it low-stakes but required.

### 2. “Model comparison map” handout or JNB

Students should practice filling in the same structure repeatedly:

| Question                               | Student answer  |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| What is the outcome variable?          |                 |
| What is the explanatory variable?      |                 |
| What is the empty model?               |                 |
| What is the complex model?             |                 |
| What statistic measures improvement?   | PRE / F / slope |
| What is the null hypothesis?           |                 |
| What was shuffled or simulated?        |                 |
| What does the p-value mean in context? |                 |
| What conclusion is reasonable?         |                 |

This is the single best support for Exam 2 because it connects XCD Chapters 2–5.

### 3. Exam wrapper / correction option

After Exam 2, allow students to recover a small amount of credit by completing corrections.

Example policy:

> Students may earn back up to 20% of missed points by submitting corrections. For each corrected problem, they must identify the mistake, show the corrected reasoning, and explain the concept in words.

This motivates learning without making the exam feel one-and-done.

## How Exam 2 fits with the project

I would use the project to **reinforce** Exam 2 topics, not replace the exam.

For example:

| Before Exam 2 | Project task                       |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Day 14        | Fit one simple model               |
| Day 17        | State a null hypothesis            |
| Day 19        | Interpret a p-value                |
| Day 21        | Submit model-comparison checkpoint |
| Day 22        | Take Exam 2                        |

Then after Exam 2:

| After Exam 2 | Project task                        |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| Day 24       | Add confidence interval             |
| Day 27       | Add second predictor if appropriate |
| Day 29       | Peer review / final presentation    |

That way the project becomes a running application of the same ideas, but the exam still verifies individual understanding.

## My suggested grading balance with Exam 2 included

| Category                                 | Weight |
| ---------------------------------------- | -----: |
| Pre-class Canvas quizzes                 |    10% |
| Mini-JNB / lab completion                |    15% |
| Post-lab HW quizzes                      |    15% |
| Exam 1                                   |    15% |
| Exam 2                                   |    20% |
| Term project + peer review               |    20% |
| Participation / reflection / corrections |     5% |

This gives Exam 2 enough weight to matter, but not so much that it overwhelms the course.

My recommendation: **keep Exam 2 on Day 22**, covering XCD Chapters **2.4–5.13/5.15**, and let the project take over after Exam 2 as the main vehicle for confidence intervals and multivariate modeling.
